list.listitem: In patients with anemia and macrocytosis, order B12 and folate levels.C
If B12 is indeterminate, order methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels.C
Oral folate or oral or intramuscular (IM) B12 supplementation is effective in reversing and preventing further megaloblastic anemia.

background.definition: Megaloblastic anemia is characterized by red blood cells (RBCs) that are larger than normal and caused by B12 or folic acid deficiency, drugs, or genetic disorders.

list.listitem: Fifteen percent over age 60 have Vitamin B12 deficiency.
Prevalence of macrocytic anemia is 1.7 to 3.9%
In one small population study, B12 deficiency (B12 <258 pmol/L) was higher in centenarians (N = 231) than in octogenarians (N = 80) (35.3% vs 22.8%, P < 0.05).
0.88 per 100,000 newborns are deficient in Vitamin B12.
In certain populations such as patients from India, B12 and folate deficiencies are higher (53% and 37% respectively).
Patients with pernicious anemia have a higher risk of hip fracture, which persists after treatment, possibly because of achlorhydria.

Patients with meglobastic anemia can have higher homocysteine levels which is associated with an increased risk of coronary artery disease. Treatment with Vitamin B12 and folate have not reduced cardiac events in individuals with elevated homocysteine. There may be a very small risk reduction for stroke with folate and B12 supplementation in the presence of elevated homocysteine.
Low vitamin B12 levels are associated with an increased risk of upper GI cancer, perhaps mediated by chronic H. pylori infection or autoimmune condition.

B12 deficiency (common): lack of intrinsic factor necessary for absorption (pernicious anemia); achlorhydria preventing release of B12 from food; inadequate dietary intake (i.e. strict vegan diet), malabsorption following gastric bypass or other gastric lesions causing gastric mucosa damage or removal of the source of intrinsic factor. A32
As many as 70% of patiets who undergo gastrectomy may develop B12 deficiency

A systematic review showed that pooled odds ratio of B12 deficiency was slightly increased in PPI users (OR1.42), but that there was significant heterogeneity in studies and association could not clearly be established.

A large cross-sectional study including 25,953 participants did not demonstrate a statistical significance between B12 and homocysteine levels in PPI users compared with non-users. However, this study did not consider length of time PPI was used and relied on patient self-reporting.
B12 deficiency (rare): bacterial overgrowth, tapeworm, tropical sprue, transcobalamin deficiency (autosomal recessive mutation of B12 transport protein).
Nitrous oxide gas is a commonly used recreational drug that may cause an acute megaloblastic anemia due to impaired B12 function. B12 levels may be normal, but homocysteine and MMA will be elevated.

Long-term metformin treatment (4 years in this study) results in B12 deficiency in about 1 of every 14 patients treated. It is not known whether asymptomatic B12 deficiency requires treatment.The authors in this study did not report the incidence of macrocytic anemia. Drop in B12 level may occur as early as 3 months after starting metformin.
Higher doses of metformin, particularly above 1500 mg daily, were more likely to result in decreased B12 levels. Supplementation may protect against this deficiency but more research is needed.

A 2016 Systematic review of diabetic patients on metformin demonstrated a drop in B12 levels during the first four months of metformin treatment and continuing through 4 years. Degree of B12 reduction was approximately 75 pg/mL
Chronic diarrhea caused by HIV/AIDS can result in B12 deficiency.
B12 deficiency is more common among hypothyroid patients.
Folic acid deficiency: dietary deficiency due to alcohol abuse, cancer, or chemotherapy (eg, 6-mercaptopurine).
In a small study of patients with macrocytosis, alcohol abuse was identified in 80% of men and 46% of women. Not all patients were assessed for other causes of macrocytosis.

Other medications that can cause megloblastic anemia. Examples include HIV medications (reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as stavudine, lamivudine, zidovudine), anticonvulsants (valproic acid, phenytoin), folate antagonists (methotrexate), chemotherapeutics (alkylating agents, pyrimidine, purine inhibitors), antibiotics (Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole), and bile acid sequestrant (cholestyramine).
B12 deficiency may occur in breastfeeding infants of mothers who are deficient in B12
Folic acid is necessary for purine synthesis; deficiency results in decreased DNA synthesis and therefore decreased red cell production.
B12 is a cofactor for the activation of folic acid; deficiency results in the same mechanism of decreased red cell production.
CBC will identify patients with macrocytic anemia.C
Folate and B12 levels will determine whether these are the cause of macrocytosis.C

B12 deficiency will cause elevations of both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; folate deficiency will only result in homocysteine elevations. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels can determine whether B12 deficiency exists in situations where B12 levels are indeterminate.B
Schilling test is not necessary since oral B12 supplementation is effective independent of the status of intrinsic factor.B

Symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency include fatigue, weakness, ataxia, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, excessive weight loss, sore tongue, depression, memory loss, and even dementia or psychosis.
The most common symptoms found in B12 deficient infants were neurologic, including irritability, lethergy, hypotonia, and movement disorders.
Folate deficiency typically causes fatigue, diarrhea, and a smooth, bright red, tender tongue. Other neuropsychiatric symptoms are uncommon.

If macrocytosis is seen on a CBC, check B12 and folic acid. If B12 or folate deficiency is suspected based on clinical signs or symptoms, do not rely on detecting macrocytosis as this is relatively insensitive. Instead, order B12 and folic acid levels directly. MCV over 110 fl more suggestive of B12 and folate deficiency than lower levels.

If B12 is indeterminate (100-400 pg/mL), order methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels. Elevation of both is diagnostic of B12 deficiency (homocysteine but not methylmalonic acid is also elevated in folate deficiency). A modest increase in methylmalonic acid may be seen with advancing age (particularly over 70 years) and with renal disease
The Schilling test to identify patients without intrinsic factor is not necessary since B12 can be absorbed without intrinsic factor when given in sufficient oral doses.
Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies can be used as surrogate markers of pernicious anemia (73% sensitivity and 100% specificity).

RBC folate has been advocated as a better measure of total body folate stores and less influenced by recent dietary intake. However, comparative studies are lacking, and it is not clear that these differences are clinically important.

Although RBC folate reflects folate levels over the life of the red cell (similar to the use of Hemoglobin A1c), there is no evidence that it is superior to serum folate in diagnosing folate deficiency
If the reticulocyte count is >2 percent, hemoloysis may be a consideration and a workup may be indicated.
In patients with symptoms suggestive of anemia, a CBC will determine whether macrocytic anemia exists.
Order B12 and folate levels; if vitamin B12 is between 100 and 400 pg/mL, order methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.
If both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are elevated, or if either is elevated and folic acid is normal, diagnose B12 deficiency. If both are normal, consider other diagnoses.
Folate deficiency: 1 to 5 mg daily will replete deficiency in 4 to 6 weeks.C
B12 deficiency: Oral B12 1000 mcg/day or 1000 mcg IM monthly will replete and maintain B12 levels.B
Oral B12 is as effective as monthly IM administration in patients with or without the intrinsic factor.This is also true in children and in those over age 65.
Oral B12 dosage: initially 1000 to 2000 mcg/day for 1 to 2 weeks. The maintenance dose is 1000 mcg/day.
IM B12 dosage: initially 100 to 1000 mcg/day or every other day for 1 to 2 weeks. The maintenance dose is 100 to 1000 mcg every 1 to 3 months.
Oral folic acid dosage: 1 mg/day (up to 5 mg/day for disorders secondary to malabsorption).
In a systematic review, in patients with Type 2 diabetes on metformin, B12 supplementation increased B12 levels and decreased homocysteine levels. It is unclear if this improved diabetic neuropathy.
For patients with moderate B12 deficiency (107-210 pmol/L) and no anemia or neurological symptoms, a randomized trial with 201 participants found no benefit to treatment.

In patients who have had gastric bypass surgery, replacement with oral B12 was comparable to IM replacement. B12 deficiency is more common following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass than in sleeve gastrectomy.
A toothpaste fortified with vitamin B-12 decreases methylmalonic acid levels in vegans and in the elderly.
If malnutrition is the cause, increasing foods with B12/folic acid is appropriate.
Oat-bran (5.2 g/day) can improve constipation and slow the decrease in B12 seen among frail, geriatric home residents.
Foods rich in B12 include, molluscs, clams, beef liver, fortified breakfast cereals, trout, salmon, beef, haddock, and tuna.
Foods rich in folic acid include breakfast cereals fortified with folate, beef liver, cowpeas, spinach, asparagus, broccoli, avocado, fortified rice, and beans.
Treatment depends on cause, and it is usually lifelong.
Megaloblastic anemia responds well to replacement with folate or vitamin B12, either orally or IM.B
Follow-up 4 to 6 weeks after beginning therapy.C
B12 deficiency is associated with an increased risk of preterm birth (OR 0.89 for each 1 SD increase in B12) and increased risk of gestational diabetes.
The USPSTF recommends that all women who are planning or capable of pregnancy take a daily supplement containing 0.4 to 0.8 mg (400-800 µg) of folic acid for the prevention of neural tube defects.
